slides.heading: Start with a sound you already own
body: Close your lips and hum through your nose. You already own this sound.
ม is that hum.
Its full name is the sound, then a word that begins with it — and that word means *horse*. Listen to the name; you will learn to write it later.

slides.heading: The trick that covers all forty-four
body: Every Thai consonant is named the same way: **its sound + a word that starts with it**.
Every first part ends on the same vowel — so you only ever listen for the consonant at the front.
ม is the **horse** letter.  น is the **mouse** letter.

slides.heading: The second hum
body: น is the hum made with your tongue at the ridge behind your top teeth.
Its name follows the same pattern, and its word means *mouse*.
Neither letter takes a puff of air. No breath after it.

slides.heading: One rope, two bollards
body: ม and น are the same shape mirrored.
**ม** — the loop hangs from the **left** shoulder.
**น** — the same loop, moved to the **right**.

slides.prompt: Without scrolling back: which of the two letters hangs its loop on the left shoulder, and what does that letter's example word mean?

slides.heading: Both letters live in the harbour
body: Both ม and น are **low class**.
Class decides tone. That is the engine of Thai spelling, and it starts in lesson 2.
In this course, low class is the **harbour** — keep both letters there.

slides.heading: The crook that follows its letter
body: า is a **long** vowel: an open *ah*, held.
It follows its consonant on the page, and never stands alone.
Vowel length changes meaning in Thai. Long and short are different vowels.

slides.heading: Listen to how flat it is
body: Every Thai syllable has a tone. Tone is part of the word's identity.
Today's syllables are all **mid tone** — flat and level.
Resist letting your pitch rise or fall. Copy the flat line exactly.

slides.heading: Your first word
body: น + า = **นา**
นา — a rice field, a paddy.
Consonant first, vowel second. This is how every Thai syllable is assembled.

slides.prompt: Build it yourself: the letter whose loop is on the right, followed by the long vowel. Say the syllable aloud — flat and level — and say what it means.

answers: Flat, mid tone. No rise, no fall.

slides.heading: Swap the front, keep the back
body: ม + า = **มา**
มา — *to come*. You will meet this verb constantly.
Same vowel, different consonant, different word.

slides.prompt: Take the word for a rice field and swap its first letter for the one whose loop hangs on the left. Say the new syllable aloud, and say what it means.

slides.heading: Close the syllable
body: น + า + น = **นาน**
นาน — *a long time*.
The same consonant can both **open** and **close** a syllable. Position decides its job.

slides.prompt: Put the mouse letter on both ends of the long vowel. Say the syllable aloud, close the ending cleanly, and say what it means.

answers: Two consonants, one vowel, three words: นา, มา, นาน.
